newsitem.title: RWANDA: Zairean rebels have complex links across region.
newsitem.headline: Zairean rebels have complex links across region.

text.p: Africa's latest guerrilla group fighting in eastern Zaire has deep-rooted, secretive and personal links with governments and armies in Rwanda, Burundi, Tanzania and Uganda, diplomats and rebel insiders say.
The relations hinge on ethnicity, ideology and personal friendship as well as strategic regional interests, they added.

The Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL), whose cutting edge is the force of Banyamulenge ethnic Tutsis now controlling much of the east, is headed by veteran Zairean rebel Laurent Desire Kabila.

Kabila is a non-Tutsi and native of mineral-rich Shaba province. He has spent time in exile in Rwanda, Zambia and Tanzania, then a base for African Marxist leaders and where he met Yoweri Museveni, at the time an ambitious young leftist.
Kabila regularly visited Uganda in the late 1980s after Museveni took power in Kampala. Museveni is known to harbour contempt for Zaire's ailing strongman Mobutu Sese Seko.

At exactly the same time, exiled Rwandan Tutsis holding top positions in the Ugandan army were fine-tuning their plans to invade their homeland. Reports denied by Rwanda say Kabila's rag-tag army took part in the invasion in 1990 from Uganda.
The link, from Museveni to Rwandan strongman Paul Kagame to the Banyamulenge is at the heart of statements by Zaire and some African states that Rwanda and Uganda back the rebellion.

Kabila's interviews are laced with anti-Western comments redolent of a bygone Cold War era. In his latest, published by the East African weekly on Monday, Kabila denied the rebels got any help from Rwanda, Burundi or Uganda.
"People get all kinds of trash from the media which want to keep Mobutu in power," Kabila said, giving his age as 55.
But foreign journalists and aid workers saw Rwandan army soldiers helping the rebels capture the Zairean town of Goma.
Insiders say Kabila, who fought Mobutu in the "Mulele" rebellion in eastern Zaire in the 1960s and the Shaba uprising in the 1980s, still travels on a Tanzanian passport.
Kabila is a former comrade-in-arms of the late Argentine-born revolutionary leader Che Guevara -- who fought with Cuban guerrillas in east Zaire in the early 1960s.
The rebel coalition is made up of four political parties with a history of unflinching opposition to Mobutu.
Kabila says the agenda is to liberate Zaire from Mobutu's 31-year rule and install democracy after a period of transition.

But analysts say that by capturing most of eastern Zaire the rebels have already achieved a key goal for the minority Tutsis in command in neighbouring Rwanda and Burundi: a friendly buffer state on the two countries' western borders which will prevent majority Hutu exiles from attacking.
Each party in the coalition has links with the four neighbouring countries. Most important is the kinship between Banyamulenge Tutsis and Rwanda's Tutsi-dominated army.
"It assures them of unlimited support and offers them a rear base unavailable to Zairean rebels in their long and little-known struggle against Mobutu," an analyst said.

Although rebels had prepared for years to take up arms and wage war against Mobutu, only an attempt by Zairean authorities this year to expel the Banyamulenge gave them a good opportunity to fulfil their ambitions.
The rebel alliance was born of a Zairean campaign to force the Banyamulenge -- a group of 400,000 or less -- back to Rwanda, a land they left up to 200 years ago.
The Banyamulenge have a solid spine of veterans who fought with the Rwandan army after it invaded from Uganda in 1990.
Like most of the Tutsi diaspora around the world, the Banyamulenge flocked to join the rebel group of Paul Kagame, now Rwanda's Vice-President and military supremo.

"It was a noble duty for the Tutsis around the world to go and join Kagame's rebel army. Most, especially the Banyamulenge, joined in 1994 at the height of Hutu genocide against the Tutsis," a diplomat said.

Last week, Kagame admitted some Banyamulenge had joined his army but had deserted to join the resistance in Zaire against deportation or even slaughter. "I am still taking stock. But we had some of them with us," Kagame told reporters.
In rebel-held territory in eastern Zaire, reporters find it hard to tell the difference between Zairean rebels and Rwandans.
Most of them speak Kinyarwanda, others speak English with strong Ugandan or Rwandan accents. Military discipline is moulded on the lines of the Rwandan army.
